title: Downward self-reducibility of PLS-complete problems
formal:
Is every PLS-complete total search problem downward self-reducible with respect to the bit length of its input? Precisely, for every binary relation \(R\) that is PLS-complete under polynomial-time search many-one reductions, must there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time oracle algorithm that finds an \(R\)-solution on every input \(x\), using an oracle for the same relation \(R\) only on strings \(z\) with \(|z|<|x|\)? It must work for every valid choice of solutions returned by that oracle.

The SODA 2026 result identifies this universal statement with \(\mathrm{PLS}=\mathrm{FP}\). This is an equivalence with an unresolved complexity-class equality, rather than an unconditional affirmative or negative resolution of the card.
why: The question tests whether a recursive structure characterizes every representation of hard local search. The newer equivalence shows that its unconditional resolution would also resolve whether all PLS problems can be solved in polynomial time.
status_note: Source-open as an unconditional yes/no target, with major subsequent classification: the SODA 2026 paper (published 7 January; open 2025 full manuscript Theorem 6 and §7.1) proves that every PLS-complete problem is traditionally downward self-reducible if and only if PLS=FP. Definitions 2.1–2.8 and the entire §7.1 conditional counterexample proof were read, along with the original ITCS definitions and Open Problem 3.4. This does not prove PLS≠FP, so no unconditional negative answer or archival resolution is claimed. Bounded later-work checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching unconditional resolution. No independent Lean formalization of the cited proof was performed.

progress.text: The source proves a canonical complete example is downward self-reducible, establishes that downward self-reducible TFNP lies in PLS, and poses the universal complete-problem question.

The full manuscript’s Theorem 6 and §7.1, published at SODA 2026, characterize the universal traditional self-reducibility statement exactly by \(\mathrm{PLS}=\mathrm{FP}\); the counterexample is conditional on inequality.

sentences: The target asks whether every PLS-complete total search relation can be solved using only shorter instances of itself.
Shorter means fewer bits in the full input encoding, and the reduction must work for every valid solution oracle.
The original paper proves the property for a canonical complete problem and places downward self-reducible total NP search in PLS.
A SODA 2026 result proves that the universal statement holds exactly when every PLS problem is solvable in polynomial time.
Its conditional negative result is recorded as progress; the card retains the unconditional yes/no question.

definitions:
A total NP search problem is a relation \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\times\{0,1\}^{*}\) with three properties. Every input \(x\) has at least one valid output \(y\) satisfying \(R(x,y)\); all such outputs have length at most one fixed polynomial \(p(|x|)\); and membership \(R(x,y)\) is decidable by a uniform deterministic algorithm in polynomial time in \(|x|+|y|\). The class of these relations is TFNP. Solving \(R\) means producing any one valid output on every input, not enumerating all outputs or selecting a preferred one. Inputs include every binary string; any malformed-instance convention must be specified as part of the relation and preserve totality.

A polynomial-time search many-one reduction from \(R\) to \(Q\) consists of uniform polynomial-time functions \(a(x)\) and \(b(x,y)\) such that
\[\forall x,y,\qquad Q(a(x),y)\Longrightarrow R(x,b(x,y)).\]
Thus every solution of the transformed instance must decode to a valid original solution. There is one oracle instance per reduction, with no promise about which solution will be returned.

PLS, polynomial local search, can be defined using the following standard circuit local-optimum problem. An instance explicitly describes positive integers \(m,r\) and Boolean circuits \(S:\{0,1\}^{m}\to\{0,1\}^{m}\) and \(v:\{0,1\}^{m}\to\{0,1\}^{r}\). Circuit outputs of \(v\) are read as unsigned binary integers. Find a string \(u\in\{0,1\}^{m}\) such that
\[v(S(u))\le v(u).\]
Circuits are finite acyclic lists of AND, OR, NOT and constant gates, with input and output wires explicitly listed; full descriptions, indices and dimensions count toward instance bit length. There is always a valid \(u\), for example any point maximizing \(v\) over the finite domain. On malformed circuit descriptions the only valid output is the empty string. This gives a total, polynomially balanced, efficiently verifiable relation. PLS consists of the TFNP relations reducible to this circuit problem by the reductions above; this is the usual polynomial-local-search class, equivalently presented by the source’s Sink-of-DAG complete problem. A relation \(R\) is PLS-complete if it is in PLS and every relation in PLS reduces to it. Completeness is not restricted to familiar combinatorial problems or any preferred encoding.

A solution oracle for \(R\) is any total selector \(O:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) satisfying \(R(z,O(z))\) for every \(z\). The selector need not be computable. Downward self-reducibility requires one deterministic oracle Turing machine \(A\) and constants \(C,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid selector \(O\) and every input \(x\), the computation \(A^O(x)\) halts within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) steps, outputs a valid \(R\)-solution for \(x\), and queries only strings shorter than \(x\). Query writing, answer reading and ordinary computation are charged; the oracle’s computation of an answer is not. Later queries may depend on earlier answers. Repeated queries receive the selector’s same answer. The machine must handle every selector, rather than assume a canonical or favorable solution. In particular, on the empty input it can make no query. All programs and polynomial bounds may depend on the fixed relation \(R\), but not on its individual input or the chosen selector.

“Smaller” means strictly fewer input bits, \(|z|<|x|\). It does not mean a smaller potential value, fewer circuit variables with a longer description, or a separately chosen well-founded measure. Queries must be to the identical encoded relation \(R\), not to an interchangeable PLS-complete problem. The total polynomial bound covers the one oracle computation; it does not presume that expanding all recursive oracle calls takes polynomial time.

In the known equivalence, \(\mathrm{PLS}=\mathrm{FP}\) is shorthand for: every relation in PLS has a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm producing a valid solution on every input. This does not identify a relation with a single-valued function. The question’s quantifier order is: for every PLS-complete relation, there exist a machine and polynomial bound that work for every input and every valid solution selector.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal statement for the stated many-one reductions and strict bit-length notion. A positive answer must establish downward self-reducibility for every PLS-complete relation. A negative answer must establish a PLS-complete relation for which no such oracle algorithm exists, with the completeness and nonexistence proofs both checked. It is equivalent to settle whether all PLS problems have polynomial-time solution algorithms, provided the equivalence is also supplied or imported as a proved Lean theorem. Merely proving the existing equivalence, assuming \(\mathrm{PLS}\ne\mathrm{FP}\), or giving a counterexample conditional on that assumption does not answer the exact yes/no target. Nor does a result only about a broader size measure, a restricted family of encodings or one chosen complete problem. Asymptotic class and quantifier statements are exact; no numerical tolerance applies.

source_formulation.text: Open Problem 3.4 asks whether every PLS-complete problem is downward self-reducible.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Open Problem 3.4, interpreted using the source’s traditional input-bit-length Definition 2.17; later equivalence recorded separately

context_blocks.text: A downward self-reduction turns a problem into calls to smaller instances of itself. For a total search problem, each call always has some valid answer, but a reduction cannot choose which answer it receives. This combines a recursive structure with a requirement of robustness to all solutions.

The original paper proves downward self-reducibility for a canonical PLS-complete problem and proves that every downward self-reducible TFNP problem belongs to PLS. These statements establish an important connection, but neither says that downward self-reducibility transfers through every completeness reduction.

Input representation matters because a polynomial-time reduction may increase bit length. A query that is smaller in one presentation need not remain smaller after translating back to another complete problem. The universal target includes all binary encodings satisfying the definitions, rather than only natural examples.

The later paper proves the exact equivalence: every PLS-complete problem is traditionally downward self-reducible if and only if \(\mathrm{PLS}=\mathrm{FP}\). Its §7.1 gives a PLS-complete relation whose downward self-reducibility would force a polynomial-time solver. Therefore, under \(\mathrm{PLS}\ne\mathrm{FP}\), the answer is no. The theorem does not prove that assumption.

The equivalence changes how the original question should be understood: a universal affirmative answer would settle the algorithmic complexity of all polynomial local search, while an unconditional negative answer would prove that some such total search problem has no polynomial-time algorithm. The card keeps that unconditional target.

The 2026 paper also studies self-reductions that decrease a more general size measure. Its final discussion leaves a separate universal question for that broader notion. That question is not substituted for the original strict input-length formulation.
